LYNCHERS ON A SPECIAL TRAIN.
An Alabama Mob Determined to Hang a Negro.
Montgomery, ALA., August 16.—About four weeks ago a negro tried to rape a young white girl, daughter of Benjamin Carpenter, at Jacksonville, Calhoun county. The negro was arrested, and for two nights the jail was guarded. Thursday night a mob of 1,000 swearing they would have the negro or burn the jail, started on their errand, but the sheriff was too quick for them and shipped the negro down to Anniston. Yesterday the mob was reorganized at Anniston swearing vengeance on the negro and again the sheriff was forced to ship his prisoner to some point south of there, presumably Talladega. Late yesterday afternoon the mob had a special train chartered, cut the wires and will probably have a first-class hanging tonight.

JUST FOR FUN A Girl Throws Arsenic in the Coffee Pot—Two Victims Dead and a Third Beyond Recovery. Mary Metzdorf has confessed to having poisoned Miss Louise Broadwaters, her little brother James and her mother, Catherine, at Baltimore. She said she put arsenic in the coffee pot with that intention, but did it "just for fun." Though not quite 17 years old, she bears herself like a hardened criminal. Miss Broadwaters died almost immediately after drinking of the coffee, and James, her six-year-old brother, expired shortly after. Mrs. Metzdorf, the third victim, is still in a critical condition. She was slightly improved Saturday, but the death of the boy caused a relapse. The coroner's injury came to the conclusion that the girl was guilty, though, according to Maryland law, her confession can not be accepted as evidence, the Court of Appeals having recently decided that a confession to a police officer by a prisoner while confined is presumably obtained by other than fair means, and is therefore not valid. Aside from this, however, the evidence against her is conclusive, and conviction almost certain. ROBBED THE MAILS.
and the Discovery of Stolen Articles In His House.

Sam Knight, the driver of a mail wagon, was arrested at Memphis, Sunday morning for robbing the United States mails. Knight has been in the employ of Contractor Wilson, of the mail service, for five months, his duty being to drive to the trains that arrived during the night and convey the mail to the post-office. Since he took charge various packages of value that had been entrusted to the mail began to miss their destination, and an investigation showed the blame to be located in Memphis. Inspector F. D. Pell, of the Postal Service, with the assistance of Postmaster Patterson, began working on the case last week, and, after a thorough investigation, settled the crime of stealing from the mails on Sam Knight, and he was accordingly arrested. A search of his residence disclosed various articles of merchandise that had been missing from the mails hid in a closet, the evidence against him thus being complete.

Wholesale Murders of Infants.

During the past week the bodies of

During the past week the bodies of eight murdered infants have been found in Memphis, Tenn., and the discoveries have been of a most ghastly nature. So far the authorities have taken no steps to capture the murderers. The newspapers are demanding an investigation and calling upon the officials to either take some action toward bringing the villains to justice or resign. A mass meeting of citizens to raise funds to prosecute the investigation is being agitated, and meets with much favor.

Aeronaut Killed.

Charles Cosgrove, an aeronaut, was instantly killed at Portland, Ore., while making a parachute descension. Cosgrove made a successful ascension in a balloon to the height of 1,000 feet, at which distance the parachute was dosened. When about 200 feet from the ground he lost his hold and fell, landing on a paved street. He was mangled almost beyond recognition.

Original Package Liquor in Iowa.

Seizures of original package liquor were made in Iowa immediately on the signing by the President of the new law. Attorneys for the saloon men claim they are illegal, as the Iowa law against such importations was set aside by the Supreme Court decision, and that the new National law does not operate to restore the annulled State law.

Killed While Raking Hay.

While Howard, the thirteen-year-old son of John McDowell, of Second Creek, near Parkersburg, W. Va., was raking hay, the horse became frightened and threw the boy in front of the rake. Several of the teeth penetrated the boy's skull into the brain, inflicting mortal wounds.

Double Murderer Surrenders.

William Jenkins arrived Sunday morning from his ranch, sixty miles from Colville, Wash., and surrendered to the authorities. He stated that he had killed two men, Wm. Daly and Benjamin Shaw, in a dispute over a horse trade. Jenkins claims that he acted in self defense.

Crap Shooter Killed.

At Bangor, Ala., forty miles above Birmingham, Sheriff A. H. Morris, of Blount, and posse made a raid upon a den of negro crap shooters, when a desperate fight ensued. A negro named Jim Thomas was killed and several others slightly wounded. The sheriff received a flesh wound.

Sarah Althea's Costs.

Sarah Althea Terry will have to pay $2,667, the costs of her late suit to recover a portion of the Sharon estate. This will strip her of part of the property left by Judge Terry, and will probably discourage her from appealing to the Supreme Court.

A Monster Hydrangea.

Geo. D. Gibbons, of Zanesville, O., reports having a hydrangea in bloom that measures fifty feet in circumference and nine and a half feet in height.

John Boyle O Reilly Dead.

John Boyle O Reilly poet and editor

John Boyle O Reilly Dead.
John Boyle O'Reilly, poet, and editor of the Boston Pilot, died Sunday, it is supposed from an overdose of chloral taken for insomnia.

An epidemic of hog cholera provails

Eog Cholera Raging.

An epidemic of hog cholera prevails in Springfield Township, Clark County, O., a territory wherein farmers lost many hogs last year by the same disease.

Russian Prince Killed.

Seven persons were killed by the bursting of the steam-pipe on the Russian man-of-war Tehesma the other day. Among the victims was Prince Khiloff.

A Baron Killed.

Baron Leon, of Vienna, has been killed by falling over a precipice in the Alps.

Gin Lee's Predicament.

Congress in 1882 passed a law inhibiting the admission of Chinese to citizenship. Since then a number of Chinese have received naturalization papers from the probate court of Franklin County, O., and have voted. Gin Lee, who received papers in 1889, and applied to the State Department as a citizen, for a passport to visit China and return, has been refused on the ground that he is not a citizen.

New Palace for the Pope.

The Pope will build a palace in the Vatican for a summer residence.

Negroes Assassinated. ABERDEEN, Miss., Aug. 4.—Eight miles east of this place, last night, while a party of colored people were returning from church on foot, they were fired upon from ambush with a gun loaded with buck-shot, by an unknown person. A woman named Susan Henry was instantly killed, and her husband, Ben Henry, was seriously wounded. It is not known whether the assassin struck the persons intended, nor what could have been the motive for the deed. The officials believe they have a clew, upon which they are now at work, but will not divulge it. The perpetrators of the dastardly crime, however, will be hunted down and brought to justice. NOTED FOR THEIR SUCCESS Henry J. Davison, Who Recently Be came Interested in the City's Progress. Alexander Metzger's Career of Industry and Usefulness in Business Ended by a Slow Disease from Which He Has Long Suffered.
The New York Times contains a sketch of the late Henry J. Davison, sr., who was a member of the new gas syndicate of this city. His Christian qualities of character, his unselfish devotion to the happiness of others and his fondness for young people are dwelt upon at length. Of his business career it is said:

"Upon his return to this country he turned his attention especially to the construction of gas-works. In this undertaking he met with his usual success, and it was so satisfactory to himself that contracts of this kind continued ever afterward to be his specialty. About 1870 he contracted for and built the works of the People's Gas-light Company of Baltimore. The work was done in an entirely satisfactory manner, and when the time came for the organization of the consolidated company of that city those who had remembered his services in the individual company naturally looked to him to organize the joint interest and to place it firmly upon the market. He became interested in the manufacture of water gas, and having convinced himself that the new process would bring profit to those who might engage in it, he gathered a few capitalists together and companies were formed for the manufacture of the new gas. From the time that he undertook the construction of gas-works opportunities were frequently presented to him for restoring companies that had been mismanaged and for putting corporations engaged in this manufacture upon a substantial financial basis. One of his most notable experiences in that line was in Brooklyn, where he induced his friends to obtain certain valuable franchise rights and to organize the Fulton Municipal Gas-light Company. He contracted with this company for the erection of water-gas-works of the capacity of 500,000 cubic feet. In 1880, a year after these works were finished, their capacity was increased to 1,000,000 cubic feet, and in 1882 to 3,000,000 cubic feet.

"The success secured with water gas led Mr. Davison to give his attention to experiments which had been made by the same inventor for the manufacture of gas from lime. He employed this invention in the construction of the plant of the Equitable Gas-light Company of this city. He built the works of the Chesapeake company, of Baltimore, in which his new processes were also employed. His next enterprise of importance was the organization of the Equitable Gas-light and Fuel Company of Chicago, for which he constructed the plant. From the financial connections that he made at that time and from the opportunities that were then presented to him he developed the Chicago Gas Trust, of which he was a leading promoter. He had the contract for building the Memphis Gas-light Company's plant, in which the lime process was employed, and of which he was especially proud because of the gratifying results which followed. He undertook also the consolidation of the gas companies of Indianapolis, and was one of the syndicate of four to purchase the companies outright and place them on the market. This purchase included not merely the city plant, but it covered also a great portion of the natural-gas fields within thirty miles of the city of Indianapolis. The new consolidated company which he and his friends thus started was fully equipped for supplying that city with gas for all conceivable purposes. When the property thus reorganized was in condition to invite investment it was not necessary for Mr. Davison to advertise his wishes, but by letters to a few capitalists he was able within one week to get subscriptions to the amount of more than $4,000,000, which was all the money that was required for the enterprise."

The Liberals Once More Ahead in Salt Lake City. SALT LAKE CITY, August 4.—The struggle for the county ticket between the Liberals and the Mormons and the Union Workingmen's Annex has been one of the fiercest ever known here. Estimated returns at 11 o'clock p. m. indicate the success of the Liberal ticket by 200 to 300 majority. ODD FELLOWS MEET They Take Possessism of the City by the Lake. THEIR NATIONAL ENCAMPMENT. The Rebeckah Lodges and the Patriachs Militant Monopolize Attention—Ceremonials and Pleasures Alternate.
CHICAGO, August 4.—The Odd Fellows and Patriarchs Militant hold possession of Chicago. Every section of the United States is represented.

Lieutenant General Underwood, Grand Sire of the order and Commander of the military branch of the Patriarchs Militant, sent over half a million letters and circulars relative to the cantonment and in many other ways called attention to the great event.

Contests in the civil branches of the order began early today and will continue throughout the week. Most of these will be held in Battery D armory and will be opened only to the initiated.

The merit contests in the work of the Rebeckah degree, in the woman's department were gallantly given the precedence and began this morning. The proceedings were opened by "Queen of the Lakes" Rebeckah Degree Lodge No 212, of Chicago.

The prizes for which the Rebeckah lodges are competing number eleven, and aggregate in value $1500. The lodges competing from outside of Chicago are from Viroqua, Wis., Columbus, Ohio, Richmond, Ind., Minneapolis, Minn., Bloomington and Omaha.

At 3 p. m. the only public ceremony took place. This was the hoisting of the American, the Canadian and the Militant flags. This was the official signal that the cantonment had begun. It was the intention to raise all the flags at the same instant and a signal for that purpose was given by General Underwood, but General Cable was determined that the stars and stripes should go up first.

A grand concert was in progress tonight and a magnificent reception and ball was given at the Battery D armory, under the auspices of the Rebeckah's degree.

Susan Henry, one of the party, was instantly killed, and her husband, Ben Henry, seriously wounded. It is not known what could have been the motive for the deed. It also says that Minister Mizner's correspondence has not been tampered with and that the minister has for days been in free communication with the United States government.

ELISABETH, N. J., August 5.—A desperate fight occurred at a picnic of Arbetter Turnverein at Ellis grove last night, nearly one hundred men taking part in the fray. Six policemen were badly handled by the infuriated anarchists during the riot. The American flag, which floated from the staff at the entrance to the grove, was torn down and trampled under foot. Warrants are out for a dozen of the rioters.

WASAINGTON, Aug. 5.—It took just ten minutes this morning for the house committee on elections to adopt a report declaring that Representative Breckenridge was not elected from the second district of Arkansaw.

BOSTON, August 5.—The directors of the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe declared a 2¾ per cent. income bonds out of the earnings of the road for nine months ending June 30. The interest is payable in September.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Aug. 5.—Returns from all over the state indicate a large democratic victory.

WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 5.—Official rough count by census bureau shows population of Philadelphia to be 1,004,894.

SPRINGFIELD, August 5.—Gov Fifer to day signed the World's fair bill. It goes into effect at once.

ALBERDEEM, Aug. 5.—Near mills, at east Alberdeen Sunday night, while a party of colored people were returning from church they were fired upon from ambush. Susan Henry was killed instantly, her husband John Henry was seriously wounded. It is not known what the motive for the deed was. Efforts are being made to hunt down the perpetrators of the crime.

MARFA, Aug. 5.—News was brought in by the foreman of the mines at Shafter, of the ambushing by Mexicans of a party of miners, a party of rangers and deputy sheriffs yesterday. Graves Stall, a ranger, was instantly killed and a deputy sheriff and deputy Marshal were seriously wounded. The fire was returned and it is believed one Mexican was killed and several wounded. The miners and rangers have about 100 Mexicans surrounded and are guarding them until further assistance can be had, when they will pick out those connected with the shooting and bring them to Marfa for safe keeping. The trouble is said to come from lynching a Mexican some months ago.

AUBURN, Aug. 5.—The best judgement possible to be found with the information at hand is that Kemmler will be executed to-morrow morning.

PARIS, Aug. 5.—Two men who were hurt by the explosion of fire damp in the Ville Beuf pit at Stelinne yesterday, died.

WORCESTER, Mass., August 5.—Cabin et manufacturers representing nearly all the important mills in the country, appointed at a meeting yesterday, a committee to devise a plan of consolidation.

WASHINGTON, August 5.—Henderson, of Georgia, explained that the Pacific railroad claims were not provided for in bill while he believed time was near at hand when their claims would have to be settled. The committee has been practically unanimous in refusing to provide for their payment when they were still pending in the courts of the country. Rodgers, of Arkansas, attacked the speaker in his rulings. He said under these rulings of the house was given the speaker power to stifle debate, gag the house, force the passage of bills to avoid exposure, outrage and mistreat the ministry and bulldoze the majority. He had degraded the majority with the full assurance of part of the Republican members that should this scheme break down under the judgment of liberty-loving people they would perish like Samson under the ruins. That if he succeeded in that, he alone should reap all glory. Henderson, of Georgia, defended the speaker against the attack made upon him. Rogers referred to him as the mighty man from Maine and declared he stood to-day as to-morrow in history a grand figure. This is the age of legislative victory and reform. Commenting on the legislation of the session Henderson touched upon the tariff bill saying although some Republicans might have desired to amend it by reason of organized opposition on the other side the time has been so consumed that these amendments could not be made. It seemed as though the minority was bent upon preventing all amendments.
Breckenridge of (Ark.) criticised the code of rules and proceeded to contrast the personal and political relation which existed between Speaker Carlisle and the members and that which existed between them and Speaker Read. In the last congress the members of the minority were always treated with courteously. Now members of the minority rising for recognition did not get the treatment they should receive at the hands of the speaker. He then proceeded to make an earnest appeal against the force bill and said to the gentlemen of the north, why shall we not come together. You cannot hold power here by mercinaries put at the polls, you cannot keep political power by debauching the ballot, Cox or jury Cox. You cannot make the country one by turning out members who are elected by the people and seating those elected by your votes. What you can do is this. You can aid the people of the south to build up that country. You can help us keep in the line of progressive march so that your sons may come and live among and intermarry in our families, so that while there will still be north and south it will be loving and rich.

The senate proceeded to the consideration of the tariff bill pending. Cerry addressed the senate on the general subject of tariff legislation. He denied that that the question had been finally settled at the last presidential election.
